etymology: Coined in 1956 by the British psychiatrist Humphry Osmond, in correspondence with Aldous Huxley, from Greek psychē (soul, mind) + dēlos (manifest, visible): "mind-manifesting." Osmond introduced it publicly to the New York Academy of Sciences in 1957 for drugs such as LSD and mescaline. By 1966–67 it named the whole visual and musical style built around those drugs: swirling day-glo posters, light shows, feedback-drenched rock ("psychedelic rock"), and the clothes to match.
biblical_def: Psychedelic describes the hallucinogenic drugs of the 1960s — LSD, mescaline, psilocybin — and the art, music, and fashion that tried to reproduce their effects: melting color, distorted shapes, music that seemed to come from inside the skull. The word means "soul-revealing," and that is its claim: that chemicals can open the mind to a truer reality. The Christian observation: Scripture names this practice and judges it. Among "the works of the flesh" Paul lists "Idolatry, witchcraft" (Gal 5:20), and the Greek word behind witchcraft is pharmakeia — the use of drugs for spiritual experience. The psychedelic promise is an old one: eat, and your eyes shall be opened. The apostle’s command runs the other way: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1Pe 5:8). God does reveal the soul and transform the mind, but by His Word and Spirit, not by a tab: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). Paul sets the two side by side: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). A grandparent who remembers the posters and the light shows has seen the art of a counterfeit Pentecost. Today the same drugs are being marketed again, this time as medicine and as spiritual practice, and a family needs the old word and the old warning.
webster_summary: Boomer-era word (coined 1956, Osmond) for mind-altering hallucinogens and the swirling art and music built on them — the pharmakeia Scripture lists with idolatry and witchcraft (Gal 5:20).
webster_full: PSYCHEDELIC, adj. (coined 1956; Boomer slang 1960s) 1. Of drugs: producing hallucinations and altered perception, as LSD, mescaline, psilocybin. 2. Of art, music, or dress: imitating or evoking the experience of such drugs — vivid swirling color, distortion, sensory overload. "A psychedelic poster." n. A psychedelic drug.
From Greek psychē, soul, mind + dēlos, clear, manifest.
Decode for families: the 2020s revival ("psychedelic therapy," "plant medicine," microdosing) uses the same drugs and the same spiritual claim with a lab coat on.
scriptures: Gal 5:20
Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies,
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
corruption_summary: The psychedelic claims that drugs reveal the soul and open the doors of perception; Scripture names drug-induced spiritual experience pharmakeia, witchcraft, and commands sobriety and the renewing of the mind by the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Huxley borrowed his book title, The Doors of Perception (1954), from William Blake, and the claim behind the psychedelic movement was always religious: the drug cleanses the doors, and you see God, or the universe, or your true self. Leary called LSD a sacrament and founded a church around it. Scripture has a precise name for that sacrament. Pharmakeia — from which we get pharmacy — appears among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20) and among the sins that shut men out of the holy city (Rev 21:8, where the "sorcerers" are pharmakoi). The Bible does not condemn medicine; it condemns seeking spiritual experience through drugs, because that is seeking God on terms He has forbidden and opening the soul to powers He has not sent.

The Christian alternative is not a duller mind but a sober and a filled one. "Be sober, be vigilant" (1Pe 5:8) is not the counsel of the uptight but of the watchman. And Paul’s contrast in Eph 5:18 shows that God means to fill the mind, not empty it — with His Spirit, through His Word, so that the believer sees more clearly, not less. The renewed mind (Rom 12:2) needs no chemistry to perceive that the heavens declare the glory of God.
roots_summary: Greek psychē (soul) + dēlos (manifest) → psychedelic, coined 1956 by Humphry Osmond → 1966–67 psychedelic art, rock, and fashion.
roots_lines: Greek psychē — breath, soul, life, mind
Greek dēlos — visible, clear, manifest
Greek pharmakeia — drug-use, sorcery; rendered "witchcraft" in Gal 5:20 (KJV)
1956–57: Humphry Osmond coins psychedelic (to Aldous Huxley; New York Academy of Sciences)
1966–67: psychedelic posters, light shows, and rock (San Francisco, London)
usage: "Grandpa’s old record has a psychedelic cover that hurts to look at."
The psychedelic promised open doors of perception; Scripture calls it pharmakeia (Gal 5:20).
Be not drunk, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).

etymology: From trip in the sense of a drug experience, especially on LSD (American slang from the mid-1960s, from the older sense of a journey), + adjectival -y. Trippy is attested from the late 1960s for anything that resembles or suggests a drug trip — disorienting, surreal, hallucinatory — and has outlived its origins: Millennials and Gen Z use it freely of films, music, and optical illusions with no thought of LSD.
biblical_def: Trippy means strange, disorienting, dreamlike — literally "like being on an acid trip." A grandparent used it of a light show; a grandchild uses it of a movie plot or a video filter. The Christian observation: the word is mostly harmless in a child’s mouth, but it carries a memory worth explaining. It praises distortion. It calls the mind’s confusion an experience to be enjoyed. Scripture’s description of the intoxicated mind is less romantic: "Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things" (Pro 23:33), and of Israel’s drunken leaders, "they err in vision, they stumble in judgment" (Isa 28:7). The trippy is the perception of a mind that cannot trust its own eyes. God wants His children to see clearly, and He gives them a better use for the mind’s attention: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things" (Php 4:8). Creation is strange enough without chemical help — a sky full of stars, a sea that roars, a body fearfully and wonderfully made. A father can enjoy a good optical illusion with his children and still teach them that the mind God gave them is a lamp, not a toy.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (late 1960s) for anything that resembles a drug trip — disorienting, surreal; now used loosely by every generation, but rooted in praise of the distorted perception Scripture describes as erring in vision (Isa 28:7).
webster_full: TRIPPY, adj. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–present) Resembling or suggestive of a hallucinogenic drug experience; bizarre, surreal, disorienting. "That movie was trippy." "A trippy light show."

Webster (1828) — TRIP, noun A stroke or catch by which a wrestler supplants his antagonist. And watches with a trip his foe to foil. 1. A stumble by the loss of foot-hold, or a striking of the foot against an object. 2. A failure; a mistake. Each seeming trip and each digressive start. 3. A journey; or a voyage. I took a trip to London on the death of the queen. 4. In navigation, a single board in plying to windward.
Decode for families: in a grandchild’s mouth it usually just means "weird and cool." In a grandparent’s memory it meant LSD.
scriptures: Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things.
Isa 28:7

But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, they are out of the way through strong drink; they err in vision, they stumble in judgment.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
corruption_summary: Trippy turns the confusion of an intoxicated mind into an aesthetic to be enjoyed; Scripture describes that state as erring in vision and stumbling in judgment (Isa 28:7).
corruption_paragraphs: The word quietly reverses a moral judgment. Before the 1960s, to see things that were not there was a symptom — of fever, drink, or madness. The counterculture made it a destination, and trippy became a compliment. Proverbs had described the experience exactly, and not as a compliment: strange sights, a perverse tongue, and the drinker’s refrain, "when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again" (Pro 23:35). The trip always promises a little more than it delivers, and so it must be sought again.

Most children who say trippy today mean nothing worse than "surprising." A wise parent does not police the word; he tells its story, and points to the better wonder. "Wine is a mocker" (Pro 20:1), and so is every substance that promises to show you more than God has shown. The mind is for thinking on what is true (Php 4:8).
roots_summary: Old French triper (to skip, to dance) → English trip (a light step; a journey) → 1960s trip (a drug experience) → late-1960s trippy.
roots_lines: Middle Dutch / Old French trippen, triper — to skip, to tread lightly
English trip — a light step; a stumble; a short journey
Mid-1960s American slang: trip — a hallucinogenic drug experience; acid trip
Late 1960s: trippy — like a drug trip
2000s–2020s: generalized to anything surreal or mind-bending
usage: "Grandpa said the lava lamp was trippy. My little sister said the same thing about a TikTok filter."
They err in vision, they stumble in judgment (Isa 28:7) — the trip described honestly.
Think on whatsoever things are true (Php 4:8).

etymology: From trip (a drug experience, American slang from the mid-1960s) qualified by bad. In the LSD culture of 1966–70 a bad trip was an experience of terror, paranoia, or panic under the drug, sometimes lasting hours and occasionally producing lasting psychosis; "bum trip" was a synonym. By the 1970s it was used figuratively of any frightening or miserable experience.
biblical_def: A bad trip was the dark side of the psychedelic experience: hours of panic, paranoia, hideous visions, the terror that one had gone mad and would never come back. The phrase then spread to mean any miserable ordeal. The Christian observation: the bad trip is not an accident of the drug culture but its confession. Every intoxicant promises one thing and delivers another, and Scripture had already written the review: "At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder" (Pro 23:32). "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Pro 14:12). Many of the Boomer generation came home from a bad trip changed — some broken, some sobered, some converted. In the Jesus Movement of the early 1970s, a striking number of testimonies began, "I was on a bad trip and I cried out to God." The Psalmist knew that cry: "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears" (Psa 34:4). The fear of the bad trip is the fear of a mind left to itself, without anchor. God’s gift is the opposite: "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). A sound mind is not the absence of experience; it is a mind held by its Maker.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (mid-1960s) for a terrifying experience under LSD or another drug, hence any miserable ordeal — the bite of the serpent Proverbs promised at the last (Pro 23:32).
webster_full: BAD TRIP, n. (Boomer slang, c. 1966–present) 1. A frightening, panicked, or psychotic reaction to a hallucinogenic drug. 2. fig. Any distressing or unpleasant experience. "That job was a bad trip." Syn. bum trip, bummer.

Webster (1828) — TRIP, noun A stroke or catch by which a wrestler supplants his antagonist. And watches with a trip his foe to foil. 1. A stumble by the loss of foot-hold, or a striking of the foot against an object. 2. A failure; a mistake. Each seeming trip and each digressive start. 3. A journey; or a voyage. I took a trip to London on the death of the queen. 4. In navigation, a single board in plying to windward.
Decode for families: when a grandparent says "that was a bad trip," he may be speaking literally. Ask gently.
scriptures: At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
Psa 34:4
I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.
corruption_summary: The drug culture treated the bad trip as bad luck; Scripture treats it as the promised end of the way that seemeth right (Pro 14:12), and answers its fear with the sound mind God gives (2Ti 1:7).
corruption_paragraphs: The counterculture had an answer for the bad trip: better "set and setting," a calmer room, a guide, a different dose. It never asked whether the whole enterprise was the problem. Proverbs does: the drink that "moveth itself aright" in the cup "at the last ... biteth like a serpent" (Pro 23:32), and the deceived man still says, "I will seek it yet again" (Pro 23:35). The bad trip was not a malfunction; it was the bill.

Yet God used it. The terror of a mind coming apart drove many young people of that generation to the end of themselves, and there they found that the God of Psalm 34 hears. A father telling this story to his son need not hide the grandparent’s past; he can show how grace met it. The spirit of fear is not from God; power, love, and a sound mind are (2Ti 1:7).
roots_summary: Middle English badde + trip → mid-1960s LSD slang bad trip → figurative "any ordeal."
roots_lines: Middle English badde — evil, worthless (origin uncertain)
English trip — a journey; mid-1960s, a drug experience
c. 1966: bad trip / bum trip in the LSD culture
1970s: figurative — any frightening or unpleasant experience
Scripture: Pro 23:29–35 — the intoxicant that bites like a serpent
usage: "Grandpa said his bad trip in 1969 was the night he started reading the Gospel of John."
At the last it biteth like a serpent (Pro 23:32).
I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears (Psa 34:4).

word: Turn On, Tune In, Drop Out
pronunciation: TURN ON, TOON IN, DROP OWT
etymology: The slogan of Timothy Leary, the former Harvard psychologist turned LSD evangelist, first spoken publicly at a press conference in New York in September 1966 and proclaimed to the crowd at the Human Be-In, San Francisco, January 14, 1967. Leary later said the phrase had been suggested to him by the media theorist Marshall McLuhan. Turn on meant to take psychedelic drugs; tune in, to harmonize with the world around you; drop out, to detach from school, career, and society. Leary insisted he meant the last as self-reliance; the young heard it as quitting.
biblical_def: Turn on, tune in, drop out was the creed of the psychedelic counterculture in six words: take drugs, follow your inner experience, and walk away from school, work, family, and responsibility. Thousands of young people did exactly that. The Christian observation: each of the three verbs has a godly counterpart, and the slogan inverts all of them. To turn on was to chemically alter the mind; Scripture says, "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). To tune in was to follow inner experience; Scripture says to tune in to God’s Word, and warns that "Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom" (Pro 18:1) — the man who withdraws to follow his own desire is the fool of Proverbs, not the sage. To drop out was to abandon work and duty; Scripture says, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10), and "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). There is a biblical kind of dropping out — "be not conformed to this world" — but it is a departure from sin, not from duty, and it moves the believer toward his neighbor, not away from him. A grandparent who dropped out in 1967 and came back can tell a grandchild the truest version of the slogan: turn to Christ, tune in to His Word, and drop the sin that so easily besets you.
webster_summary: Timothy Leary’s psychedelic slogan (1966–67): take drugs, follow inner experience, abandon society — three verbs Scripture inverts: be transformed (Rom 12:2), hear God’s Word, and work heartily as to the Lord (Col 3:23).
webster_full: TURN ON, TUNE IN, DROP OUT, slogan (Timothy Leary, 1966–67) The counterculture’s call to use psychedelic drugs (turn on), attend to one’s inner experience and surroundings (tune in), and withdraw from conventional society, education, and employment (drop out).

Webster (1828) — TUNE, verb transitive To put into a state adapted to produce the proper sounds; as, to tune a forte-piano; to tune a violin. TUNE your harps. 1. To sing with melody or harmony. Fountains, and ye that warble as ye flow Melodious murmurs, warbling tune his praise. So we say of birds, they tune their notes or lays. 2. To put into a state proper for any purpose, or adapted to produce a particular effect. [ Little Used .]
Decode for families: each verb survives separately — turned on (aroused, excited), tuned in (alert, aware), dropout (one who quits school).
scriptures: Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Pro 18:1
Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
corruption_summary: Leary’s slogan made drugs the door, the self the guide, and withdrawal the goal; Scripture makes the renewed mind the door, God’s Word the guide, and faithful work the calling.
corruption_paragraphs: Leary marketed a religion. He called LSD a sacrament, founded the League for Spiritual Discovery in 1966, and preached a gospel of inner liberation that asked nothing of the convert but a dose. Its fruit was a generation of young people who left school and family to live in crash pads, many of whom never fully returned. The slogan’s genius was that it sounded like spiritual seriousness — tune in, wake up, leave the rat race — while it was really the oldest temptation in the book: separate yourself, follow your desire, and call it wisdom (Pro 18:1).

The gospel also calls men out. But it calls them out of darkness into His marvelous light, out of sin into service, and out of the self into the body of Christ. The Christian does not drop out of his duties; he does them "heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23). He does not turn on with a chemical; he stays "sober" and "vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). And he does not tune in to himself; he tunes in to the voice that says, "This is my beloved Son: hear him."
roots_summary: Turn on (1960s, to take drugs) + tune in (radio) + drop out (to quit) → Leary’s slogan, September 1966 press conference and January 14, 1967 Human Be-In.
roots_lines: Turn on — 1960s slang: to take a drug; to excite (from switching on a device)
Tune in — from radio: to adjust to a frequency; hence to become attuned
Drop out — to withdraw from school or society; dropout (n.) by 1930
September 1966: Leary’s New York press conference; League for Spiritual Discovery
January 14, 1967: proclaimed at the Human Be-In, San Francisco
usage: "Grandpa says he turned on, tuned in, and dropped out for about six months, then Grandma made him get a job."
If any would not work, neither should he eat (2Th 3:10).
Be transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2), not by altering it.

etymology: From the phrase blow one’s mind, which entered American slang in the mid-1960s for the effect of a hallucinogenic drug (to shatter one’s ordinary perceptions), and quickly broadened to mean to astonish or overwhelm. Mind-blowing as an adjective is attested from 1967; mind-blower and the shorter mind-blown followed. The Beatles’ "A Day in the Life" (1967) contains "He blew his mind out in a car," a deliberately double-edged line.
biblical_def: Mind-blowing means overwhelming, astonishing, beyond what the mind can take in — and in 1967 it meant, literally, what an LSD trip did to the mind. Grandchildren now say "mind blown" of a magic trick or a science fact. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of the thing this word reaches for, without the chemicals. There is knowledge that genuinely exceeds the human mind, and it is the knowledge of God. David: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Psa 139:6). Paul, at the end of eleven chapters of doctrine, does not conclude; he erupts: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" (Rom 11:33). He prays that believers would "know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge" (Eph 3:19). The Lord Himself says, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways" (Isa 55:9). The difference between that wonder and the drug’s is that God’s overwhelming does not destroy the mind but enlarges it, and it is true. The 1960s sought a mind blown open by chemistry and got confusion. The believer meets a mind lifted by truth and gets worship. If a child is looking for something mind-blowing, open the Gospel to the empty tomb.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (1967; from blow one’s mind, of LSD) for astonishing, overwhelming — a wonder Scripture finds in the knowledge of God, too high to attain (Psa 139:6), which enlarges the mind instead of shattering it.
webster_full: MIND-BLOWING, adj. (Boomer slang, 1967–present) 1. Originally, producing hallucinatory or mind-altering effects, as a drug. 2. Overwhelmingly impressive, astonishing, or surprising. "A mind-blowing concert." Also blow one’s mind (v. phr., mid-1960s); mind-blown (adj., later).

Webster (1828) — BLOW, verb transitive preterit tense blew; participle passive blown. [Latin flo, to blow This word probably is from the same root as bloom, blossom, blow a flower.] 1. To make a current of air; to move as air; as, the wind blows. Often used with it; as, it blows a gale. 2. To pant; to puff; to breathe hard or quick. Here is Mrs. Page at the door, sweating and blowing. 3. To breathe; as, to blow hot and cold.
Decode for families: "mind blown" in a child’s text means "wow." Give them something worth the word.
scriptures: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Eph 3:19
And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.
Isa 55:9
For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
corruption_summary: The 1960s sought an overwhelmed mind through drugs and called it revelation; Scripture offers the true overwhelming — the depth of the riches of God — which ends not in confusion but in doxology.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase began as a description of damage. To blow the mind was to break its ordinary operation, and the drug culture prized the breakage as a doorway. Wonder was confused with derangement. That confusion is still with us whenever astonishment is sought as a sensation for its own sake — the next bigger spectacle, the next louder concert, the next more shocking fact.

Scripture keeps wonder tethered to truth. Paul’s "O the depth" (Rom 11:33) comes after careful argument, not instead of it. The wonder rises out of understanding and runs beyond it. "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1Co 2:9). That is the only genuinely mind-blowing sentence, because it is about the only thing too big for every mind — and true.
roots_summary: Old English myne / gemynd (mind) + Old English bláwan (to blow) → mid-1960s blow one’s mind (of LSD) → 1967 adj. mind-blowing.
roots_lines: Old English gemynd — memory, thought, the mind
Old English bláwan — to blow, as wind; later, to burst or shatter
Mid-1960s: blow one’s mind — to undergo or cause a hallucinogenic experience; to astonish
1967: mind-blowing, adj.; later mind-blower, mind-blown
Scripture: Psa 139:6; Rom 11:33 — knowledge too wonderful to attain
usage: "Grandma thought the moon landing was mind-blowing. She was right."
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! (Rom 11:33).
The love of Christ passeth knowledge (Eph 3:19) — the wonder that enlarges the mind.

etymology: From freak (Old English frician, to dance, is doubtful; more likely a dialect word for a sudden whim or caprice, 1560s) + out. Freak out appears in mid-1960s drug culture for a panicked or wildly excited reaction, and was put on the map by Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention’s debut album Freak Out! (1966). By the 1970s it meant simply to panic, to lose one’s cool, or to become extremely upset — the sense every grandchild knows. Chic’s disco hit "Le Freak" ("Freak out!", 1978) made it a dance-floor shout.
biblical_def: To freak out is to lose control — to panic, to fly into a rage, or to come unglued with fear or excitement. In 1966 it described a reaction to drugs; by 1978 it was a disco chant; today it is how every teenager describes his parents’ reaction to a dented fender. The Christian observation: the word names a real and common experience, and Scripture addresses it with tenderness and with command. The disciples freaked out in the boat on the Sea of Galilee while the Lord slept; He rose, said to the sea, "Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm" (Mar 4:39), and then turned to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" (Mar 4:40). The antidote to freaking out is not a technique but a trust: "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" (Psa 56:3). "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus" (Php 4:6–7). The promise is not that storms will never come but that a mind "stayed on thee" will be kept "in perfect peace" (Isa 26:3). A father who does not freak out when his son confesses a failure has preached that sermon without words.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (mid-1960s; Zappa’s Freak Out!, 1966) for losing control in panic, anger, or excitement — answered by the Lord who stilled the storm and asked, "Why are ye so fearful?" (Mar 4:40).
webster_full: FREAK OUT, v.i. and v.t. (Boomer slang, mid-1960s–present) 1. To react with sudden panic, anger, or wild excitement; to lose emotional control. 2. To cause someone to do so. "Don’t freak out." "The noise freaked me out." n. freak-out, an episode of losing control; originally a drug-induced one.

Webster (1828) — FREAK, noun 1. Literally, a sudden starting or change of place. Hence, 2. A sudden causeless change or turn of the mind; a whim or fancy; a capricious prank. She is restless and peevish, and sometimes in a freak will instantly change her habitation.
Decode for families: one of the most durable Boomer words — your children use it daily.
scriptures: Mar 4:39
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
Mar 4:40
And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?
Psa 56:3
What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
corruption_summary: The word normalizes the loss of self-control as an ordinary reaction; Scripture treats fear and rage as storms the Lord commands to be still, and the mind stayed on Him as kept in perfect peace.
corruption_paragraphs: In the 1960s the freak-out was half a goal. A good concert, a good dose, a good happening was supposed to make you lose control. The ecstatic loss of self was prized. By the time the word reached the suburbs it had lost the glamour and kept the license: freaking out became a normal, even expected, way to respond to bad news. Scripture does not share that expectation. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit, not a symptom of repression.

But Scripture is gentle with the frightened. The Lord did not leave the disciples in the boat; He got up. Paul does not merely say "Be careful for nothing"; he says what to do instead — pray with thanksgiving — and promises a peace that guards the heart (Php 4:6–7). The grandparent who teaches a grandchild Psalm 56:3 has given him something better than "calm down."
roots_summary: 16th-c. English freak (a sudden whim, caprice) → 19th-c. freak (an oddity) → mid-1960s freak out (drug panic) → 1970s general "lose control."
roots_lines: 1560s English freak — a sudden turn of mind, a caprice (perhaps from Old English frician, to dance)
19th c.: freak — a malformed creature; freak of nature; the circus freak show
Mid-1960s: freak out — a panicked or ecstatic reaction, especially on drugs
1966: Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention, Freak Out!
1978: Chic, "Le Freak" — "Freak out!" as a disco shout
usage: "Don’t freak out, Mom, it’s just a scratch."
Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? (Mar 4:40).
What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee (Psa 56:3).

etymology: From space (Latin spatium), probably by way of the 1960s drug sense of being "out in space," i.e. disconnected under the influence of marijuana or LSD; spaced out and spaced are attested from the mid-to-late 1960s, followed by spacey / spacy (c. 1968). The Space Age (Sputnik 1957, the moon landing 1969) gave the image its currency. In later use it means simply dazed, absent-minded, or not paying attention.
biblical_def: To be spaced out is to be mentally absent — dazed, drifting, not really there. In 1968 it usually meant high; now it usually means distracted, the glazed look of a teenager four hours into a screen. The Christian observation: Scripture calls the believer to the opposite state, and calls it repeatedly. "Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1Pe 1:13). To gird up the loins was to tuck the long robe into the belt so a man could run; the mind is to be gathered, not drifting. "Be sober, be vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Mat 26:41) — said to disciples who could not stay awake one hour. Paul adds the reason: "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:15–16). The spaced-out mind is not merely wasting time; it is unguarded. Our grandparents’ generation got there with chemicals. Our children are getting there with feeds and notifications. The cure is the same: a mind gathered under Christ, present to God, to neighbor, and to the duty in front of it.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (mid-to-late 1960s) for dazed or disconnected, originally from drugs, now from distraction — the opposite of the girded, sober, watchful mind Scripture commands (1Pe 1:13; 1Pe 5:8).
webster_full: SPACED OUT, adj. (Boomer slang, mid-1960s–present) Dazed, stupefied, or disconnected from one’s surroundings, originally as from drugs; later, inattentive or absent-minded. Also spaced; spacey; to space out (v.), to lose focus.

Webster (1828) — SPACE, noun [Latin spatium, space; spatior, to wander. This word is probably formed on the root of pateo.] 1. Room; extension. space in the abstract, is mere extension. Pure space is capable neither of resistance nor motion. 2. Any quantity of extension. In relation to bodies, space is the interval between any two or more object’ as the space between two stars or two hills The quantity of space or extent between bodies, constitutes their distance form each other. 3. The distance or interval between lines; as in books. The space in music are named as well as the lines.
Decode for families: "Sorry, I spaced" = "I forgot." The screen has replaced the joint as the leading cause.
scriptures: Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Spaced out treats mental absence as a pleasant drift; Scripture treats it as an unguarded mind and commands the believer to gird up the loins of the mind, be sober, and redeem the time.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1960s made being spaced out a pleasure to be sought: drift, float, let the world go by. The danger is that the drifting mind is the easiest mind to capture. The adversary walks about "seeking whom he may devour" (1Pe 5:8), and the lion takes the straggler, not the alert. Our Lord’s disciples slept in Gethsemane, and within hours one had denied Him three times.

The modern version is subtler. No one smokes anything; the phone does the work. But the effect is the same — a mind that is everywhere and nowhere, a person present in body and absent in soul. Paul’s word circumspectly means looking around carefully, eyes open. A family that sets down the screens at the table and attends to one another is practicing Eph 5:15–16.
roots_summary: Latin spatium → Old French espace → English space; Space Age imagery + 1960s drug slang → spaced out, spaced, spacey.
roots_lines: Latin spatium — room, extent, interval
Old French espace → Middle English space
1957–69: the Space Age (Sputnik to Apollo 11) makes "out in space" a common image
Mid-to-late 1960s: spaced out, spaced — dazed by drugs
1970s–present: space out, spacey — absent-minded, inattentive
usage: "Sorry, Dad, I totally spaced out during the sermon."
Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober (1Pe 1:13).
Walk circumspectly, redeeming the time (Eph 5:15–16).

etymology: Of imitative origin, from zonk, a sound-word for a heavy blow (compare bonk). Zonked appears in American jazz and beat slang of the late 1950s meaning drunk or stoned ("zonked out of his mind"), and was common in 1960s drug culture. By the 1970s it chiefly meant exhausted, asleep, out cold — the sense in which grandparents still say "I’m zonked."
biblical_def: To be zonked is to be knocked out — originally by drink or drugs, now usually by sheer exhaustion. "The kids were zonked by eight o’clock." The Christian observation: the word holds two kinds of collapse, and Scripture treats them very differently. The first, the drugged stupor, is the state the drunkard of Proverbs lives in, and God warns against it. The second, honest exhaustion, is something God tenderly provides for. He made the body to need sleep, and He gives it: "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). Sleep is an act of faith — "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psa 4:8). The man who works himself zonked every night may be telling God he does not trust Him to keep the world turning while he rests. Yet there is a third kind too, the sluggard’s: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth" (Pro 6:10–11). Scripture honors the tired worker, rebukes the idle sleeper, and offers to both something better than collapse: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). The Lord renews strength (Isa 40:31); He does not merely knock us out.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (late 1950s jazz / beat) first for drunk or stoned, later for utterly exhausted — Scripture rebukes the drugged stupor and the sluggard’s slumber, but gives His beloved sleep (Psa 127:2) and rest in Christ (Mat 11:28).
webster_full: ZONKED, adj. (Boomer slang, late 1950s–present) 1. Intoxicated by alcohol or drugs; stupefied. 2. Utterly exhausted; fast asleep. "I was zonked by nine." Also zonked out; to zonk out, to fall asleep suddenly.
From imitative zonk, the sound of a heavy blow.
Decode for families: in a grandparent’s mouth today it almost always means "tired."
scriptures: It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
Pro 6:10
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep:
Pro 6:11
So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Zonked blurs the drugged stupor, the sluggard’s slumber, and the worker’s honest weariness; Scripture separates them, and offers the weary rest in Christ rather than collapse.
corruption_paragraphs: The beat generation used zonked admiringly: to be zonked was to be gone, past caring, beyond reach. That is the one sense Scripture never blesses. The drunkard of Proverbs wakes from his zonk only to say, "I will seek it yet again" (Pro 23:35). Stupor is not rest; it is escape, and it leaves a man more tired than it found him.

The modern sense — worn out — is more sympathetic, but it hides its own danger. Our culture often runs on exhaustion as a badge of importance, collapsing at night and starting again at dawn. Psalm 127 calls that vanity. God gives His beloved sleep; He does not require them to earn it by running themselves into the ground. The Sabbath is His standing argument against the zonked life: a day each week when the world keeps turning without our help. And the Lord Jesus offers the rest beneath all rest: "Come unto me" (Mat 11:28).
roots_summary: Imitative zonk (the sound of a heavy blow) → late-1950s jazz / beat slang zonked (drunk, stoned) → 1970s zonked (exhausted).
roots_lines: Imitative zonk — a blow, a thud (compare bonk, conk)
Late 1950s jazz and beat slang: zonked — drunk or high
1960s drug culture: zonked out — stupefied
1970s–present: zonked — exhausted, fast asleep
Scripture: Psa 127:2 (sleep as God’s gift) against Pro 6:10–11 (the sluggard’s slumber)
usage: "After the church picnic, Grandpa was zonked in the recliner by four."
He giveth his beloved sleep (Psa 127:2).
They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31).

etymology: From Jimi Hendrix’s "If 6 Was 9" (1967): "I’m gonna wave my freak flag high," and above all from Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young’s "Almost Cut My Hair" (1970): "I feel like letting my freak flag fly." The freak flag was the long hair, beard, and wild dress that marked a man as one of the counterculture’s "freaks" — a word the hippies had reclaimed as a badge. Let your freak flag fly is still used for openly displaying one’s eccentricity.
biblical_def: One’s freak flag is the visible sign of being different — in 1970, the long hair that said "I am not one of you"; today, any eccentricity a person refuses to hide. Let your freak flag fly means: be unapologetically yourself. The Christian observation: Scripture actually calls believers to be visibly different, but it locates the difference somewhere else entirely. "Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light" (1Pe 2:9). Peculiar there means a people for God’s own possession, and their difference is meant to show forth His praises, not their own uniqueness. Paul says plainly, "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10) — there is a holy oddness, and the world will notice it. But the freak flag flies for the self. Its message is "look at me," and Proverbs has a sharp word for that impulse: "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself" (Pro 18:2). The test is the one Paul applies to himself: "do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The hippie refused to please his parents and sought instead to please his peers. The Christian refuses to make pleasing men his aim at all. That is a flag worth flying.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (Hendrix 1967; CSNY 1970) for the long hair or wild dress that marked a counterculture "freak"; hence any proudly displayed eccentricity — a self-display Scripture sets against the "peculiar people" who show forth God’s praises (1Pe 2:9).
webster_full: FREAK FLAG, n. (Boomer slang, 1967–70) The long hair, beard, or flamboyant dress by which a hippie ("freak") displayed his rejection of mainstream society; hence any outward sign of nonconformity. Let one’s freak flag fly — to display one’s eccentricity openly and without apology.

Webster (1828) — FLAG, noun An ensign or colors; a cloth on which are usually painted or wrought certain figures, and borne on a staff. In the army, a banner by which one regiment is distinguished from another. In the marine, a banner or standard by which the ships of one nation are distinguished from those of another, or by which an admiral is distinguished from other ships of his squadron. In the British navy, an admiral’s flag is displayed at the main-top-gallant-mast-head, a vice-admiral’s at the fore-top-gallant-mast-head, and a rear-admiral’s at the mizen-top-gallant-mast-head. To strike or lower the flag, is to pull it down upon the cap in token of respect or submission. To strike the flag in an engagement, is the sign of surrendering. To hang out the white flag, is to ask quarter; or in some cases, to manifest a friendly design. The red flag, is a sign of defiance or battle.
Decode for families: the modern equivalent is "authenticity" — the self as the thing displayed.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
Pro 18:2
A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: The freak flag makes nonconformity a display of the self; Scripture calls believers to a holy peculiarity that displays the praises of God and refuses to make pleasing men — old or young — the aim.
corruption_paragraphs: The freak flag was sold as courage — the brave individual against the gray conformist crowd. But the long-haired young man of 1970 was usually conforming exactly, to a different crowd. The flag was a uniform. That is the irony of every self-expression movement: it ends in a new set of rules about how to look different. Paul saw through it: the question is never whether you please men but which men, unless you have decided to please God (Gal 1:10).

Christian nonconformity is real and commanded: "be not conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2). But it is not achieved by hair, dress, or attitude; it is produced by a renewed mind. Its visible marks are the strangest things the world ever sees — a man who forgives, a woman who is content, a family that keeps the Lord’s Day, a young person who will not lie. Those are the peculiar people of 1Pe 2:9, and their flag is the cross.
roots_summary: English freak (an oddity; reclaimed by 1960s hippies) + flag → Hendrix "If 6 Was 9" (1967), CSNY "Almost Cut My Hair" (1970) → let your freak flag fly.
roots_lines: English freak — an oddity of nature; in 1960s slang, a hippie or an enthusiast ("jazz freak")
English flag — a banner, a standard, an ensign of allegiance
1967: Jimi Hendrix, "If 6 Was 9" — "wave my freak flag high"
1970: Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, "Almost Cut My Hair" — "let my freak flag fly"
Scripture: the "peculiar people" (1Pe 2:9) — God’s own possession, displaying His praises
usage: "Grandpa let his freak flag fly until he got a job at the bank in ’72."
Ye are a peculiar people, to shew forth His praises (1Pe 2:9) — not your own.
If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ (Gal 1:10).

etymology: Up + tight. In 1930s–50s jazz slang up tight could mean close, intimate, or in good shape ("everything’s up tight"), and Stevie Wonder’s "Uptight (Everything’s Alright)" (1965) used it in that positive sense. Almost at once the counterculture reversed it: by 1966–67 uptight meant tense, anxious, inhibited, rigidly conventional — the hippie’s word for the square. That is the sense that survived.
biblical_def: To be uptight is to be tense, rigid, anxious, unable to relax — and in the hippie’s mouth it was the worst thing a person could be: the starched-collar parent, the rule-bound dean, the churchgoer who frowned at everything. The Christian observation: the word bundles together a real sin and a real virtue, and Scripture separates them. There is a sinful uptightness — the anxiety that will not trust God, and the legalism that loads people with rules God never gave. Our Lord rebuked the Pharisees because "they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders" (Mat 23:4). The Preacher warned, "Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?" (Ecc 7:16). And Paul: "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage" (Gal 5:1). The Lord Jesus offers the true release: "my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Mat 11:30). But the hippie also called holiness uptight — chastity, sobriety, keeping one’s word, honoring parents. That is not uptightness but order, and its opposite is not freedom but chaos. The Christian is called to "moderation" (Php 4:5): neither the rigid Pharisee nor the sprawling hippie, but a man at rest in grace and firm in obedience.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (reversed c. 1966 from a jazz-era positive sense) for tense, anxious, or rigidly conventional — a word that rightly rebukes Pharisaic burdens (Mat 23:4) but wrongly brands holiness as repression.
webster_full: UPTIGHT, adj. (Boomer slang, c. 1966–present) 1. Tense, nervous, anxious. 2. Inhibited; rigidly conventional or prudish. "Don’t be so uptight." Earlier (1930s–1965) jazz sense, now obsolete: fine, in good order, close ("Uptight, everything’s alright").

Webster (1828) — TIGHT, adjective [Latin taceo; that is, close, closely compressed.] 1. Close; compact; not loose or open; having the joints so close that no fluid can enter or escape; not leaky; as a tight ship, or a tight cask. 2. Close; not admitting much air; as a tight room. 3. Sitting close to the body; as a tight coat or other garment.
Decode for families: when a child calls a rule "uptight," ask whether it is God’s rule or ours. Hold the first firmly; hold the second loosely.
scriptures: Mat 23:4
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
Ecc 7:16
Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Php 4:5
Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.
corruption_summary: Uptight rightly mocks anxiety and man-made burdens but wrongly treats every moral boundary as repression; Scripture lifts the Pharisee’s yoke and lays on the believer the easy yoke of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation needs a word for the Pharisee, and the Boomers chose uptight. They had cause: much of 1950s churchgoing respectability was more about appearances than about Christ, and Mat 23:4 describes it well. But the word overreached. It made all restraint the enemy. Modesty was uptight; marriage was uptight; sobriety was uptight. In rejecting the Pharisee’s burden the counterculture also threw off the Lord’s yoke, and found that the alternative to a heavy yoke is not no yoke but a crueler one.

The gospel answer is the yoke of Christ: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29). It is a yoke — real obedience, real boundaries — but it is easy, because it is borne with Him and from a heart at rest in His forgiveness. The believer is neither uptight nor loose. He is free (Gal 5:1), and his moderation is known unto all men (Php 4:5).
roots_summary: Old English up + Old Norse þéttr / English tight → 1930s–65 jazz up tight (fine, close) → c. 1966 counterculture reversal: tense, inhibited.
roots_lines: English tight — firmly held, close, not loose (from Old Norse þéttr, watertight)
1930s–50s jazz slang: up tight — close, intimate; in good shape
1965: Stevie Wonder, "Uptight (Everything’s Alright)" — the positive sense
c. 1966–67: counterculture reversal — tense, anxious, inhibited, square
Scripture: the Pharisee’s heavy burdens (Mat 23:4) and Christ’s easy yoke (Mat 11:30)
usage: "Grandma called Great-Grandpa uptight because he wouldn’t let her wear jeans to church."
They bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne (Mat 23:4) — the true uptightness.
My yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Mat 11:30).

etymology: From the verb phrase hang up (to suspend, to put on a hook; to delay). The psychological sense — a neurosis, inhibition, or fixed emotional difficulty that "hangs" a person — is American slang from the late 1950s, popular in beat and then hippie usage ("he’s got a hang-up about money"; "no hang-ups"). To be hung up on someone or something, obsessed with it, belongs to the same family.
biblical_def: A hang-up is an emotional snag: a fear, inhibition, obsession, or old wound that keeps a person from acting freely. "He’s got a hang-up about his father." "She has no hang-ups." The hippie ideal was to be free of all of them. The Christian observation: the word is a secular, therapeutic name for something Scripture describes more truthfully. Some hang-ups are wounds and fears, and the gospel speaks to them with healing: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (Joh 8:36). Some hang-ups are guilt that has never been confessed, and David describes that weight and its removal: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid ... and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin" (Psa 32:5). Some hang-ups are simply sin we cherish, and the writer to the Hebrews names them: "let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us" (Heb 12:1). And some of what the hippies called hang-ups were not hang-ups at all but a healthy conscience — modesty, shame at wrongdoing, fear of God. The world calls those hang-ups to be cured; Scripture calls them graces to be kept. The Christian is not called to have no inhibitions but to have the right ones, and to be released from the rest by the One who makes all things new: "old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" (2Co 5:17).
webster_summary: Boomer slang (late 1950s) for an emotional inhibition, fear, or obsession — a therapeutic word Scripture sorts into wounds Christ heals (Joh 8:36), guilt He forgives (Psa 32:5), sin to lay aside (Heb 12:1), and conscience to keep.
webster_full: HANG-UP, n. (Boomer slang, late 1950s–present) A psychological or emotional problem, inhibition, or fixation; a persistent difficulty in dealing with something. "He has a hang-up about authority." Also hung up (adj.), anxious or obsessed: "hung up on a girl."

Webster (1828) — HANG, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive hanged or hung. 1. To suspend; to fasten to some fixed object above, in such a manner as to swing or move; as, to hang a thief. Pharaoh hanged the chief baker. Hence, 2. To put to death by suspending by the neck. Many men would rebel, rather than be ruined; but they would rather not rebel than be hanged. 3. To place without any solid support or foundation. He hangeth the earth upon nothing. Job 36:1 .
Decode for families: "no hang-ups" was the hippie’s boast. Ask what a person without any inhibitions would actually be like.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Psa 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
Php 3:13
Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
corruption_summary: Hang-up lumps conscience, guilt, sin, and wounds together as inhibitions to be shed; Scripture distinguishes them, keeping the conscience, forgiving the guilt, killing the sin, and healing the wound.
corruption_paragraphs: The hippie promise of "no hang-ups" sounded like freedom and turned out to be a program for dismantling the conscience. Shame about sexual sin was a hang-up. Reluctance to take drugs was a hang-up. Respect for parents was a hang-up. The cure offered was always the same: do the thing you are inhibited about, and the hang-up will dissolve. Often it did — and the conscience dissolved with it. Paul warns of men whose conscience has been "seared with a hot iron"; the 1960s found a way to do that and call it therapy.

Scripture offers a better freedom. It does not tell a man that his guilt is a hang-up; it tells him his guilt is real and can be taken away (Psa 32:5). It does not tell him his past defines him; it tells him to forget "those things which are behind" and press on (Php 3:13). And it promises a freedom the counterculture could not give, because only the Son gives it: "free indeed" (Joh 8:36).
roots_summary: Old English hangian (to hang) + up → hang up (to suspend, to delay) → late-1950s beat slang hang-up (a psychological snag) → hung up on.
roots_lines: Old English hangian — to be suspended; hón — to hang (transitive)
English hang up — to put on a hook; to delay or stall
Late 1950s American beat slang: hang-up — a neurosis, inhibition, obsession
1960s hippie usage: "no hang-ups" as an ideal of total freedom
Also hung up (anxious; obsessed); compare the telephone hang up (unrelated sense)
usage: "Grandpa says he got rid of all his hang-ups in 1968. Grandma says he got some new ones."
Lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us (Heb 12:1).
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed (Joh 8:36).

etymology: From cop, to catch or take (18th-century thieves’ cant, perhaps from Latin capere via cap), as in cop a plea (to plead guilty to a lesser charge, American underworld slang by the 1920s–30s). Cop out, to back out or evade, appears in American criminal and jazz slang by the 1940s–50s; the noun cop-out, a weak excuse or evasion of responsibility, was everywhere in 1960s counterculture talk.
biblical_def: A cop-out is an evasion — a lame excuse, a dodge, a way of avoiding responsibility while appearing to have a reason. "Saying you’re too busy is a cop-out." The 1960s used it against the establishment ("the system’s a cop-out") and against each other. The Christian observation: the cop-out is the oldest move in the human repertoire, and Scripture records the first one. When God asked Adam whether he had eaten of the forbidden tree, "the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Gen 3:12) — blaming his wife and, behind her, God. Eve copped out to the serpent (Gen 3:13). The guests invited to the great supper "all with one consent began to make excuse" (Luk 14:18): a field, oxen, a wife. Paul says that before God every man is finally "without excuse" (Rom 1:20), and James closes every loophole: "to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin" (Jas 4:17). The gospel does not offer the sinner a better excuse; it offers him the end of excuses. "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Pro 28:13). The opposite of the cop-out is not a stronger argument but a plain confession. A father who says to his son, "I was wrong, forgive me," has taught him more than a hundred lectures on responsibility.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (from 1940s underworld cop out; ubiquitous 1960s) for an evasion or lame excuse — the move Adam made first (Gen 3:12), answered only by confession that finds mercy (Pro 28:13).
webster_full: COP-OUT, n. (Boomer slang, 1960s–present) An evasion of responsibility; a weak excuse; a compromise that avoids a hard choice. "That answer is a cop-out."
COP OUT, v.i. (1940s criminal slang; 1960s general) To avoid a commitment or responsibility; to back out. Compare cop a plea, to plead guilty to a lesser charge.
Decode for families: the first cop-out was in Eden. Teach your children the phrase "I did it, I’m sorry" before they learn this one.

corruption_summary: The cop-out disguises evasion as reason; Scripture traces it to Eden’s blame-shifting, declares every man finally without excuse, and offers mercy only to the one who confesses and forsakes his sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The counterculture was quick to spot the cop-outs of its parents — the hypocrisy of respectable people who said one thing and did another. It was slower to spot its own. "Society made me do it," "the system is to blame," "I was just being honest about my feelings" — these were cop-outs dressed as insight. The modern therapeutic vocabulary has added a whole dictionary of them. But the shape is always Adam’s: someone else, and finally God, is responsible for what I did.

God’s response to the first cop-out was not to accept the excuse but to pronounce judgment — and then, astonishingly, to promise a Redeemer (Gen 3:15) and to clothe the guilty pair with skins. Grace does not argue with our excuses; it cuts through them. The man who stops copping out and says, with David, "I acknowledged my sin unto thee" finds that the One he was afraid of is the One who forgives.
roots_summary: 18th-c. cant cop (to catch, to take) → 1920s–30s cop a plea → 1940s cop out (to back out) → 1960s noun cop-out (an evasion).
roots_lines: 18th-c. thieves’ cant cop — to catch, to seize (perhaps from Latin capere); hence cop / copper, a policeman
1920s–30s American underworld: cop a plea — to plead guilty to a lesser charge
1940s–50s: cop out — to back out, to evade
1960s: cop-out (n.) — an excuse or evasion; universal in counterculture speech
Scripture: the first excuse (Gen 3:12–13); "without excuse" (Rom 1:20)
usage: "‘I forgot’ is a cop-out, son. Try ‘I didn’t do it, and I should have.’"
The woman whom thou gavest to be with me (Gen 3:12) — the first cop-out.
